newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai targets seen attainable, more details sought.
newsitem.headline: Thai targets seen attainable, more details sought.

text.p: Analysts and economists said on Tuesday that economic targets set by Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan appeared achievable, but they debated whether his policy should carry more details.

Amnuay forecast gross domestic product (GDP) would grow 7.0-7.5 percent annually in the next few years, the current account deficit would ease to 7.5-7.9 percent of GDP in 1997, and exports were expected to rise 7-10 percent next year.

"Based on the country's track record, I would say these forecasts are achievable but it would depend on government initiatives to get the economy back on track," said Rob Sheridan, senior analyst at Thai Fuji Finance and Securities.
Amnuay made his projections as the Thai baht came under renewed pressure in overseas markets wary of Thai economic woes.

The Bank of Thailand projected the current account deficit would widen to 8.2 percent of GDP in 1996 from 8.1 in 1995, economic growth is seen declining to 6.7 percent this year from 8.6 in 1995, and exports would show zero growth this year after rising 23.6 percent in 1995.
"I think the forecasts are reasonable but I haven't really seen anything new yet," said Susheel Narula, head of research at Seamico Securities.

"We are looking for things like a budget cut and other points like opening the market further and definite times for privatisations but its been mostly talk so far," he commented on Amnuay's statement.
Analysts said Amnuay's economic projections could pave the way for a 100 basis point cut in Thai lending rates in 1997.
Olarn Chaipravat, president of the Thai Bankers Association, applauded Amnuay's policy statement, saying it included a time table for specific targets to be achieved.
"It is a comprehensive plan, especially on measures for tackling various issues including the BBC case," he said, referring to government efforts to revive the ailing Bangkok Bank of Commerce Plc.

Vicharat Vijitvathakan, president of the Association of Securities Companies, said under Thailand's financial liberalisation plan, members of his association could start undertaking foreign exchange business next year.

But analysts voiced concern that Amnuay may have to compromise his economic policies to accommodate the political interests of factions in Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's coalition government which came to power last month.
"It is important for Thailand to establish a comprehensive programme for rehabilitating the economy and it is important that personalities do not get in the way of that" Sheridan said.

Analysts said any government moves to help ailing finance and property firms by mobilising financial support from bigger, more stable firms may backfire by eroding foreign confidence in the Thai banking sector.
They said investors would see such moves as spreading rather then containing risks.

"I think it will please local businessmen...but it may not be so well received by international investors who might see it as expanding or hiding problems," said Patera Dilokrungthirapop, head of research at Crosby Securities.
